2026-09-08.headline: Score HOLDS at 27/30 for a twenty-first consecutive edition. No channel moved. One, and it is the whole judgment: the oil channel’s hold has become a choice between two rising series rather than a reading of one. The scored continuation closed $93.16 on 7 September, $1.84 below the $95 upgrade and its highest close since 24 July; the active contract closed $97.00, a fourth straight close through the level. Two closes on the scored series fires the upgrade and takes the score to 28. It is held on the continuation for a reason that is affirmative and not inertia: the upgrade, the downgrade and the pre-war anchor are all written on that series, and moving one of the three would make the channel incoherent in the other direction. §9.56 was disclosed on 2 September, before the level was straddled; the alternative reading is printed, not suppressed. Two. Five of six channels sit at the cap, so the score registers none of what the window contained — AAA diesel setting all-time highs on 4, 6 and 7 September, a blockade tally moving twice in four days, Kpler’s lowest reported traffic reading since May — and none of what cut the other way, a seventh day with no acknowledged American strike on Iranian soil. Three, and it is a limit of the instrument rather than of the market: the political channel is scored on a GASOLINE series while the records were in DIESEL, and gasoline did not follow, at 17.3% below its own 2022 record. The channel cannot see a diesel record by construction. Whether it should be scored on a distillate series is a real question and is not decided under the pressure of a record. Four. The bond market still declines to price any of it as inflation, and the honest form of that is bounded by a date: through 4 September, the last day on which either the extract’s breakeven or an independent Treasury par curve resolves, ten-year compensation was flat to two decimals. The diesel records and the $97.00 close fall AFTER it and are untested by any reading this document holds. The breakeven is UNRESOLVED on both rows of this extract — a move on a shut market, then an exact four-decimal repeat in a live one — and three rate fields the last edition published as marks are simply GONE, which is new pitfall §9.60. Meanwhile Iran’s security council and then its foreign ministry both said a Hormuz arrangement with Oman is close; Oman has published nothing on it, from a site its own footer shows was updated on 7 September. bondYield.title: MARITIME DENIAL — 5/5, held. The blockade tally moved three times in four days, the visible traffic count collapsed across three readings, and the allied product that should adjudicate it does not yet exist.
bondYield.text: (i) The state. The downgrade requires a verified reopening AND traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. (!) ‘NORMAL’ HAS NO SINGLE DENOMINATOR — Kpler’s pre-war ~130–140/day, IMF PortWatch’s 85/day — and on NEITHER does current traffic clear 25%; the nearest reading of the war is UKMTO VRA’s 22–23% to 27 August, itself twelve days stale. The leg is not close. Neither leg advanced and the traffic leg moved sharply the wrong way. (ii) The adjudicating document is MISSING, and that is the honest description. No JMIC Update 095 exists at the cut on a direct read of ukmto.org, so 094’s frozen count of 101, cut off at 051500Z, is SILENT on 6, 7 and 8 September and cannot be used to test anything that happened in them. It is PROSPECTIVE, not NOT OBTAINED (§9.46). The only UKMTO product since is ADVISORY 127-26 of 6 September, which JMIC maps onto the three tankers the UNITED STATES struck — so the newest item in the maritime record is the American action, not an Iranian one. (!) Iran’s 5 September claim to have struck three tankers is therefore UNCORROBORATED into a fourth day, and the correct statement is that no allied product records it, not that no such attack occurred. (iii) The traffic leg deteriorated on the one series that publishes daily, and the readings cannot be joined. Kpler published three ten-day moving averages of visible commodity vessels — above 15 on 4 September, about 13 on the 5th, 10 on the 6th — and calls the last its lowest since May, publishing no numeric May baseline, so the superlative is the PROVIDER’S and is not independently checkable. (!) A ten-day mean cannot move five points in two sessions, so these are not one series: each is reported as a separate provider reading and NO rate of change and no direction is computed across them (§9.24). There is no 7 or 8 September reading from any provider. (iv) A CLAIM THIS DOCUMENT CARRIED IS WITHDRAWN. Last edition said no VLCC had exited since 2 September. Kpler still says that of its VISIBLE universe; Windward’s AIS-plus-dark log records a 340-metre VLCC-class tanker outbound on 4 September, dark, at reduced speed, trailing a 16km sheen. A dark hull cannot appear in a visible count, so the two are reconcilable and the unqualified form was wrong. The claim is re-issued as no VISIBLE VLCC exit since 2 September (§9.19, §9.24). (v) THREE CENTCOM-dated readings in four days, two moves: 87 on 3 September, 92 on 6 September, 94 on 7 September, with disabled and boarded unchanged at 3 and 2 throughout. (!) The point is not the seven vessels. It is that JMIC 094 cited 87 as the latest available official figure on the day it published, when CENTCOM’s own count was already 92 — the allied summary is a lagging record of the American operation, and this document will not treat it as a check on it.

bondYield.title: OIL PRICE SHOCK — 2/5, held. A fourth close through the level on the active contract, and the scored series closed to $1.84 — its nearest approach since it was last above the line in July.
bondYield.text: (i) §9.56 has run out of mitigating detail. The active contract has now closed above $95 on FOUR consecutive sessions — $95.63, $95.52, $96.28, $97.00 — the last being the highest active close since 22 May, and the first run of four since a twenty-close run ended on that date. Two closes is this instrument’s own definition of a sustained break. Applied to COA, the upgrade condition was met on the 3 September close — five days ago. (ii) Applied to CO2, the series the rule has always been read on, it has not: the continuation closed $93.16, +$0.84, $1.84 below the level. But that is now the nearest this series has closed to $95 since it was last ABOVE it on 24 July, and it narrowed from $2.68. On 3 September the two series moved apart, which made the hold comfortable; on 7 September they moved together, and the gap has narrowed 45% across two sessions — $3.37, $2.68, $1.84. (iii) The rule is NOT moved, and there is an AFFIRMATIVE reason as well as a procedural one. The affirmative reason: the $95 upgrade, the $72.48 downgrade and the $72.48 pre-war anchor are ALL written on the continuation, so moving the upgrade alone to COA would leave the downgrade and the anchor on a different series and make the channel incoherent in the other direction. The procedural reason: moving it now would be moving it to the series that fires it, six days and four closes after the document disclosed the problem in the open. That is exactly what §9.26 forbids and what §9.16 anticipated. The score is held, the alternative reading is printed in the tape, in the score grid and in the watchlist, and a reader who checks a screen quote for ‘Brent’ will find $97.00 and can see why. (!) What would settle it is not an argument but a print: two CO2 closes above $95 fires the upgrade on the rule as written, and $1.84 is roughly two sessions’ worth of the recent move — the largest daily change on this series in the last four sessions is $0.84. (iv) The basis is stable and neither leg is a signal. Brent’s ran 3.89, 3.96, 3.84, 3.88 across 3–8 September — a narrowing then a part-retrace, with no second step and no sign change; WTI’s went 2.91 on 4 September to 3.07 on the 8 September mark, a widening, with no 7 September value at all. (!) Two contracts moving opposite ways across the same span for a second consecutive edition is an argument against reading either basis as a market signal. §9.41 clears; §9.36 still forbids constructing anything across the two Brent series. (v) The move is not being made in the Gulf alone. OPEC+ held October output UNCHANGED on 6 September, and its stated reason was that it must first review member capacity to set 2027 baselines — a process, not a barrel. (!) No quantified OPEC+ spare-capacity figure dated 4–8 September was published or found, and none is scheduled — an absence in the record rather than a pending release or a retrieval failure. The September STEO is due 9 September and the WPSR 10 September, both delayed by the holiday.

bondYield.title: US INFLATION IMPULSE — 5/5, held. The count of closes above the firing level did not advance, because there was no close; and the breakeven has now failed to resolve on two consecutive rows.
bondYield.text: (i) The 5y5y forward count STAYS AT FOUR. Its last resolved value is the 4 September close of 2.3082%, 0.82 bp above the 2.30% firing level and the narrowest of the four. There was no 7 September close, so no fifth close exists and none is claimed. The 8 September mark of 2.3030% would leave 0.30 bp — but a mark decides nothing, and this document has been wrong before by treating one as though it did (§9.31). The scored downgrade, the 2.142% anchor, is 16.62 bp away and has not been approached. (ii) BE10 IS UNRESOLVED ON TWO CONSECUTIVE ROWS, FOR TWO DIFFERENT REASONS, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. On 7 September it was carried because the cash market was shut (§9.58c). On 8 September it printed 2.3536, identical to four decimal places to the 7 September cell, in a row where every nominal tenor moved — which is the pure §9.35 case, the one that concealed a war high on 17 August. Its last RESOLVED value is the 4 September 2.3532%, 9.63 bp above the 2.2569 anchor. (!) §9.48 applies and is stated rather than assumed: an exact repeat on a four-decimal derived generic is strong evidence of a carry, so the rule discriminates well here, and no d/d is asserted either way. (iii) AN INDEPENDENT SERIES SAYS THE SAME THING, AND THE HONEST FORM IS BOUNDED BY A DATE. A Treasury par-curve read puts the 10-year breakeven flat at 2.35% on 1, 2, 3 and 4 September — two decimals, so it cannot separate 2.3532 from 2.3536, and it is quoted for DIRECTION only. Through 4 September, the last date on which either the extract’s breakeven or the par curve resolves, ten-year inflation compensation was flat to two decimals against an ISM services prices-paid index at 72.6, its highest in four years. (!) The diesel records of 4, 6 and 7 September and the $97.00 close of the 7th fall AFTER that date and are UNTESTED by any breakeven reading this document holds. No inference about re-anchoring is available, and none is drawn. (iv) That is corroborated from the podium. A Federal Reserve governor said on 3 September, the last speech before the blackout opened on 5 September: his earlier worry that higher energy prices would bleed into many goods and services prices ‘hasn’t come to pass, at least so far’. He also said it may not take much acceleration to nudge him toward supporting tighter policy, and that his vote turns on August inflation. Those two sentences are the whole September debate, and they are hike-versus-hold, not hold-versus-cut. (v) The pricing supports a BAND and not a direction. Sourceable readings of the September HIKE probability, each with its own outlet and never joined: about 50% (28 Aug), 66% and 70% from two outlets (31 Aug), about 52% (4 Sep, post-payrolls), 59% (5 Sep); a prediction market read 50% on the 5th. (!) THE PRECISE PAIR THE LAST EDITION PUBLISHED — 48.4% then 58.4% — COULD NOT BE RE-VERIFIED AND THE DECIMALS ARE WITHDRAWN (§9.13). (!) NOR does a direction survive: on these numbers the 4 September post-payrolls reading is BELOW both 31 August readings, and deriving a trend from single points on three venues is the splice §9.24 forbids. September hike pricing sits somewhere in a 50–70% band and cannot be narrowed.

bondYield.title: TREASURY STRESS — 5/5, held. The volatility leg is UNRESOLVED, not satisfied a third time: MOVE has not printed for two sessions, and a stale low is not reassurance.
bondYield.text: (i) MOVE has NO PRINT for 7 or 8 September. Its last close is 73.10 on 4 September, a second consecutive close below 75 and the first below the 73.38 pre-war anchor since 28 August. The downgrade’s volatility leg is therefore satisfied on the last resolved close and UNRESOLVED thereafter — it is NOT satisfied a third session, and this document will not convert a missing print into a close. §9.9 was written for exactly this: MOVE went dark through a 10.9 bp long-end move in July and the stale low read as calm. (ii) The yield leg fails by 24.23 bp on the same close. It has not closed below 5.00% since 6 July. (!) BOUND THE OTHER HALF PROPERLY, because the last edition did not: the claim that the leg ‘has not been within 15 bp since 28 July’ is true of this regime and is NOT a war-long claim — the pre-war anchor of 4.6106% sits 39 bp INSIDE the condition, so the leg was satisfied for the whole of the period before the war. The bounded form is the only honest one. (iii) (!) THE ANOMALY IS UNRESOLVED RATHER THAN PRESENT, and the distinction matters. On the last resolved closes, volatility sits 0.28 points BELOW its anchor while the 30-year sits 63.17 bp ABOVE its own. Both legs of that comparison are now stale by two sessions on one side and unresolved on the other, so it is restated as of 4 September and no live reading is claimed. (iv) The curve, on marks and across TWO sessions rather than one: 2Y +0.66 bp, 5Y +0.54, 10Y +0.41, 20Y +0.13, 30Y +0.21, with 2s10s −0.250. A mild bear flattener in shape — front-led, with the 2s10s at −0.250 consistent BY CONSTRUCTION rather than independently, since 41.144 is 4.7862 minus 4.3727. (!) It is NOT monotonic with tenor: the 30-year rose more than the 20-year. (!) And it is small: the largest move on the curve is two-thirds of a basis point across two trading sessions spanning four calendar days, which after August payrolls of +162,000 with +55,000 of upward revisions — about five times the twelve-month trailing average of +31,000, and 2.5 to 3.1 times a consensus RANGE of 53,000 to 65,000 — is itself the observation. Every war-high close set on 1 September survives; on the last resolved close the 5-year sits 1.03 bp from its own and on the 8 September mark 0.49 bp, the nearest of any tenor on either basis. (v) The supply test is running as this edition is written. A $58bn 3-year auctions on 8 September, a $39bn 10-year reopening on 9 September and a $22bn 30-year reopening on 10 September — $119bn of coupons, all settling 15 September, the first day of the FOMC. (!) Results for none of them exist at the cut. August CPI lands 11 September, inside the blackout.

bondYield.title: POLITICAL STRESS — 5/5, held. The scored series was DARK across the whole record window, and the record it could not see was set three times in four days.
bondYield.text: (i) The scored series moved AWAY from its downgrade for a fifth consecutive edition, then stopped reporting. (!) The downgrade is not a single level: it needs THREE consecutive closes at or below $4.60 with no intervening print above $4.70, so with the series dark the earliest possible move is at least three prints away. AUTMUSAG BACKFILLED to $4.93 for 4 September — a FIFTH consecutive rise and the highest print since 29 May — (!) and the last edition’s ordinal for $4.92 was one too high and is CORRECTED from a fifth to a FOURTH (§9.32), expressly NOT a war high ($5.18, 20 May). It sits 33 cents above the $4.60 downgrade condition and 18 above the $4.75 that fired the upgrade. It produced NO PRINT on 7 or 8 September and is not extrapolated (§9.30). (ii) THE RECORD KEPT FALLING WHILE THE MEASURE WAS DARK. AAA’s national diesel average set a fresh all-time high on 4, 6 and 7 September — $5.8500, $5.8970, $5.9015 — and AAA’s own highest-recorded-price table now shows the current print as the record. (!) Two housekeeping corrections follow from re-verification rather than from news. The superseded 2022 figure is no longer displayed by AAA, so this document stops asserting 19 June 2022 as its date and carries only the level. And the $5.8819 the last edition published for 5 September could not be independently re-verified and is carried as single-source (§9.13). (iii) Gasoline still does not follow. AAA regular $4.1505 on 7 September is 17.3% below its own $5.0165 record of 14 June 2022. On AAA’s own 31 August base, diesel is +30.13c on the week and regular +6.98c — 4.3 times the pace, a third consecutive edition. (!) A FOURTH retail series must not be spliced in: EIA’s on-highway diesel read $5.599 for 31 August against an EIA all-time high of $5.810, so on the EIA series the record has NOT been taken. Different survey, different universe, and its next print is 9 September (§9.19). (iv) The cause is still a refining constraint rather than a crude one, on the 28 August week: distillate stocks 104.2 mn bbl, 14% below the five-year average, against refinery utilisation of 98%, the highest since 2018; and East Coast distillate at 19.318 mn bbl, the lowest in a weekly series that begins in 1990. A Russian diesel export ban, extended on 29 August to 30 September, is a second driver and this document does not apportion between them. (v) THE LIMITATION IS A SCOPE CHOICE, NOT AN INSTRUMENT FAILURE, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS. The scored series resolved on 4 September, the FIRST of the three record days, and was dark on the 7th and 8th — so it saw one of the three and missed two. The deeper point is that AUTMUSAG is a GASOLINE series and the records were in DIESEL, and this document insists in four places that gasoline and diesel are different grades, different surveys and different universes that must never be compared. The channel cannot register a diesel record BY CONSTRUCTION, and its own §1.3 shows why: gasoline did not follow, at 17.3% below its own 2022 record. (!) Whether the political channel should be scored on a distillate series is a real question and is NOT decided here, because re-basing a trigger onto the series that would move it is what §9.21 and §9.56b forbid.

bondYield.title: ESCALATION RISK — 5/5, held. Iran escalated in words from three institutions in three days and in deeds not at all; Oman is again the missing signature, for a second edition.
bondYield.text: (i) THE KINETIC RECORD SINCE 5 SEPTEMBER IS EMPTY AND THE RHETORICAL ONE IS NOT. No CENTCOM release since 5 September on a direct read of its index; no acknowledged US strike on Iranian SOIL since 1 September, a seventh day; and no Iranian attack on any Gulf state since 3 September. (!) Bound both. The window is NOT kinetically quiet — US forces destroyed three Iranian tankers on 5 September, Iran claims three more, UKMTO logged disabling fire on the 6th and Jizan was struck on the 7th. And the tanker Downy was struck at the Kharg anchorage on 5 September, inside Iranian territorial waters, so the soil claim is a soil-versus-waters distinction rather than an absolute; no damage ashore was reported. (ii) Against that emptiness, three Iranian principals in three days: the parliament speaker on 6 September that the era of proportionate responses is over and that American oil and gas companies across these waters ‘share that exposure’; the security-council secretary on 7 September that the posture toward US warships and bases has been ‘fundamentally recalibrated’; the acting defence minister on 8 September, answering US claims that Iran cannot reach the blockading warships, ‘you will see the results’. This edition it fired on TWO cells, both for 3 September and both UPWARD: AUTMUSAG to $4.92, two cents above the value carried and the highest since 29 May though NOT a war high, WIDENING the political distance to 32 cents; and SOFR to 3.66, resolving the non-backfill the last edition recorded. The test has now fired UPWARD on the scored gasoline series in FIVE consecutive editions — $4.83, $4.86, $4.90, $4.92 — against a downgrade case that was live a fortnight ago.

protocol.step: Compute deltas and test every trigger
protocol.detail: d/d, w/w five rows back, and versus pre-war; explicit trigger tests for the four market channels plus Stage-4 A, B and C. Run min, max and last-prior-occurrence on the full column before writing ANY superlative (§9.32). This edition that discipline established that $2.68 is the nearest reading since 21 August and NOT of the war; that Threshold B’s six-close run IS the longest of the regime; that Henry Hub’s discount is the smallest since 8 July; and — the correction — that the count of active-contract closes above $95 published last edition was one too high.

protocol.step: Verify the news, and re-verify what was inherited
protocol.detail: Every claim needs a named source and an exact date, and negative claims decay fastest of all (§9.23). State the exact query behind every negative. Say NOT OBTAINED rather than estimating, and distinguish it from PROSPECTIVE (§9.46). (!) This edition the discipline paid in the other direction: the last edition’s ‘no sanctions landed’ and ‘tanker for tanker is one anonymous chain’ were both true at their cut and both were overtaken within hours, so they are SUPERSEDED rather than withdrawn. A negative that expires is not a negative that was wrong, and the two are recorded differently.

protocol.step: Build, then QA in three passes
protocol.detail: A numeric harness against the dataframe; a STYLE harness measuring bold ratio and headline length (§9.52, §9.55); an adversarial PROSE pass by reviewers with no access to the source data, run as TWO reviewers CONCURRENTLY against the same pre-fix text and merged into one patch (§9.42); and a VISUAL render, which is not optional (§9.43). Re-run the numeric and style harnesses AFTER the prose fixes. Balance the bold tags in every fragment after every edit (§9.42a). Check the page budget at build time, not after the prose is final (§5A).

The edition and the annex go into the project root together. A file that is not committed never reaches the reader. The annex does not go into the dashboard PDF folder, because the score-history script regexes a score sentence out of every PDF there and the annex has none. Then snapshot the fragments under a date-stamped name, at the END of the run, so no edition can overwrite another’s sources.

methodology.scale: Six channels, each scored 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch; 8–14 stress; 15–21 systemic-risk watch; 22–30 crisis. Maritime denial and escalation risk are event channels; oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress and political stress are market channels scored on confirmed closes.
methodology.scaleCap: (a) Confirmed closes only for market channels. No market channel moves on an intraday print. The 8 September snapshot moves nothing — including an active-contract mark of $97.20 that is through the trigger level, and a TTF mark of €73.990 that is ABOVE the war-record CLOSE and is not reported as a record. (!) THAT DISCIPLINE WAS TESTED IN THIS EXACT WINDOW AND PAID: the last edition’s TTF mark of €74.855 was also above the record, nothing was claimed on it, and it settled €1.549 LOWER and BELOW the record. (b) Hysteresis, and it is now being tested from the other side. Upgrades fire on a sustained break; downgrades require a sustained reversal past a wider threshold. The 5y5y forward closed BELOW its own firing level on 28 and 31 August and two editions came under pressure to redefine the downgrade to meet it; the rule was NOT moved, and the forward has closed ABOVE the level on 1, 2, 3 and 4 September. (!) THE COUNT STAYS AT FOUR THIS EDITION: 7 September produced no close, so no fifth is claimed. The fourth cleared by 0.82 bp, the tightest of the four, and a margin inside one session’s typical move is not clearance. The rule is not rewritten now that it is thin, for the same reason it was not rewritten when it was broken (§9.16, §9.26). (c) The scale saturates in BOTH directions (§9.7, §9.27). FIVE of six channels are at the cap, so the score could not register US retail diesel setting three fresh all-time highs in four days, Hormuz traffic at its lowest visible reading since May, a blockade tally moving three times in four days, or a second consecutive edition in which Iran announces a bilateral Hormuz instrument with no counterparty text. methodology.intraday: §9.56 — NOW FOUR CLOSES OLD, AND THE SCORED GAP HAS HALVED IN THREE SESSIONS. A trigger written on a continuation series stops being well-defined the moment the basis opens, and the failure is silent. The oil channel’s upgrade is ‘Brent above $95 sustained’. That rule was written and applied through long stretches in which CO2 and COA printed the SAME NUMBER — most recently exactly zero for twenty consecutive sessions to 28 August. Earlier rolls opened a basis too; what is new is a roll that opened one STRADDLING the trigger. Brent rolled on 31 August and the basis ran 2.12, 3.08, 3.54, 3.89, 3.96, then 3.84 and 3.88. On the 7 September close the trigger falls BETWEEN the two series for a FOURTH consecutive session: the scored continuation is $1.84 below it and the active contract $2.00 ABOVE it. ‘Sustained’ has a settled operational meaning here — two consecutive confirmed closes, the test that fired US-inflation 4→5 on 31 July and cut oil 2→1 on 3 July. The active contract has now closed above $95 FOUR times in succession, so on that series the upgrade condition is met in full and has been since the 3 September close. (!) THE MATERIAL CHANGE THIS EDITION IS THE SIZE OF WHAT IS LEFT. The scored gap has run $3.37, $2.68, $1.84 across three sessions, and $1.84 is the nearest this series has closed to its trigger since it was last ABOVE it on 24 July. The hold rests on nothing except which of two rising series the rule happens to be written on, and the remaining gap is narrower than the series’ own recent daily range. That is stated plainly rather than dressed up: what settles this is not an argument but two closes. Three things follow and all three remain the practice. (a) The channel is held on the scored continuation, and the alternative reading is published in the EDITION rather than buried here, because a reader checking a screen quote for ‘Brent’ will find the active contract. (b) The rule is NOT moved to whichever series would fire it — the §9.26 discipline. (c) The problem is disclosed as an open methodological question and NOT decided under the pressure of a fired trigger, which is the §9.16 precedent. The general form, which will recur: any threshold expressed as an absolute level on a rolling series has an undefined region as wide as the basis, and the basis is zero exactly when nobody is looking at it. ¶ §9.51 — CARRIED FORWARD, UNCHANGED AND UNSETTLED, and STILL six observations deep because 7 September produced no close. When a defective test is met a second time by a different mechanism, record the MECHANISM, not a verdict. §9.49 recorded Threshold B’s 28 August arming as a defect: a long-end stress test tripped by an 11.14 bp front-end move in which the 30-year contributed 1.25 bp. On 31 August B held on a bear STEEPENER in which the 30-year contributed the largest move on the curve; on 1 September on a bear FLATTENER in which it contributed the smallest; on 2 and 3 September on a BULL STEEPENER twice; and on 4 September on a bear flattener again, in which the 30-year was the ONLY tenor to FALL. (!) The run did NOT extend this edition: there is no 7 September close, so the ordinals are unchanged and the seventh is decided on 8 September. (!) The written test has now returned the same answer through three of the four configurations available, in both directions, and on the latest occasion it was satisfied while its own long-end leg moved TOWARD the threshold, the margin narrowing 4.65 to 4.23 bp — the test held open by the leg it was not written about. That is not ambiguity observed twice but six times, and it strengthens rather than resolves the original complaint. (!) A second observation sharpens it further, and it is new this edition: the two legs DIVERGED for the first time in the run — the 30-year margin narrowed a third consecutive close to 4.23 bp while the 10-year’s WIDENED to 13.21 bp — so a single test is now being held open by the leg it was not written about. The open question is unchanged and is not settled here: whether B should be conditioned on a long-end CONTRIBUTION rather than a long-end LEVEL. ¶ Restatements and comparability. Vendor restatements are normal and make absolute levels non-comparable across editions, though directional analysis is continuous. A contract roll does the same thing to a continuation series silently, which is why the basis check is a standing check. The dual gasoline series is never re-based: AUTMUSAG is the scored reference and preserves the $3.52 anchor and the $4.75 trigger; USRFRUSA is corroboration only; AAA’s published headline is a third series and is never compared with either. The pre-war anchor is the 27 February 2026 close, re-verified field by field every edition; it is unchanged to date. FOUR OPEN ITEMS REMAIN DISCLOSED RATHER THAN DECIDED. (1) FIRST IN LINE AND SHARPER THAN LAST EDITION: §9.56, the oil trigger’s ambiguity across the roll — $2.68 below on the scored series and $1.28 through on the active one, with three consecutive closes through on the active series and, for the first time, both series moving the same way. (2) Threshold B’s long-end LEVEL versus long-end CONTRIBUTION question, per §9.49 and §9.51, now six observations deep with diverging legs and a narrowing 30-year margin. (3) §9.57, the reconciliation of the scored gasoline series to any published construction, open and un-advanceable this edition. (4) The US-inflation channel’s firing-versus-downgrade gap, no longer dormant: the firing trigger has held four closes but the margin has narrowed to 0.82 bp while the downgrade sits 16.62 bp lower. The oil channel’s own separate asymmetry stands unchanged: its downgrade is written as a mediated pause AND ‘a close’ at or below $72.48 while its upgrade requires a SUSTAINED break, which as written makes the downgrade’s PRICE limb easier to trip than the upgrade’s, though the downgrade also requires a mediated pause and is not therefore the easier test overall. It is $19.84 away and not live.

bondYield.title: MARITIME DENIAL — 5/5, held. The adjudicating product is missing for a second edition, and this document has to correct what it said the last one contained.
bondYield.text: (i) The state. The downgrade requires a verified reopening AND traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. (!) ‘NORMAL’ STILL HAS NO SINGLE DENOMINATOR, and the test is run ONLY where one provider supplies BOTH the numerator and the baseline (§9.19, §9.24). On Kpler’s own figures, 6 vessels against a pre-war ~130–140/day is under 5%. On PortWatch’s own, 7% of its ~85/day base. On the last OFFICIAL volume basis — 4.9 mb/d in Q2 against 21.6 mb/d pre-conflict — it is 22.7%, the nearest reading to the leg that exists and a QUARTERLY figure, stale by a quarter. Windward and Lloyd’s List publish no baseline, so the test is UNTESTABLE on them and no cross-provider ratio is constructed. (!) JMIC’s 59/48h is a US-FACILITATED SUBSET, not total traffic, and is not divided by anyone’s baseline. Neither leg advanced. (ii) A CORRECTION THIS DOCUMENT OWES ITS READER, AND IT IS A DENOMINATOR ERROR OF EXACTLY THE KIND §9.19 EXISTS TO STOP. The last edition described JMIC 094’s 101 as a frozen transit count. It is not a transit count at all: it is the CUMULATIVE CONFIRMED-INCIDENT total since 1 March. 094’s transit figure is 59 vessels across the 3–5 September 48 hours, US-facilitated. Every sentence built on ‘101 says nothing about 6, 7 or 8 September’ was directionally right and numerically about the wrong series, and the correct statement is that 094 is cut off at 051500Z and therefore silent on both the incident count AND the transit count for 6–9 September. (iii) (!) JMIC Update 095 is NOT OBTAINED, a second consecutive edition. The method, stated once: three direct URL probes for update numbers 095, 096 and 097 on 9 September, all 404, against a JS-driven index that renders nothing. THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT CLAIM 095 DOES NOT EXIST. A 404 on a guessed URL plus a non-rendering index is exactly the evidence class that made the last edition’s CENTCOM negative false — that release was reachable only with an explicit page parameter — and a negative built on an index must be probed a second way before it is published (A2.3.7). The honest state is non-retrieval, not non-existence. The consequence is sharper than last edition: 094 does not record the American strikes of 8 September either, so the allied maritime record now omits the largest single kinetic event of the window. (iv) The traffic leg is unchanged in level and better characterised in structure, because a second provider published a same-day count. Windward logged 12 transits on 6 September, seven inbound and five outbound, with ZERO dark crossings; Kpler logged 6 for the same day on visible AIS-active commodity vessels, and separately a ten-day MEAN of 10 that it calls its lowest since May on no published numeric baseline. (!) These are not a discrepancy and they do not average: Windward counts AIS-transmitting cargo and tankers, Kpler counts commodity vessels only, and a same-day two-to-one spread between them is a definitional artefact (§9.24). (!) Kpler’s 15+, 13 and 10 across 4–6 September are NOT one series and are not printed as a sequence: the first two are daily counts and the third is a ten-day mean, which is why a five-point fall in two sessions is arithmetically impossible. No rate of change and no direction is computed across them. There is no 7, 8 or 9 September reading from any provider. (v) CENTCOM’s tally is 94 redirected, 3 disabled, 2 boarded as of 7 September, issued on its X account rather than by release, and no 8 or 9 September figure was found. (!) The ‘100 ships’ milestone that appears in search belongs to 23 MAY and to a different counting basis; joining it to this series would manufacture a jump that did not happen.

Two sessions ago the arithmetic of ‘more than twice a normal day’ was the reason to expect nothing imminent; that reason is gone, and saying so is the point of restating the same test each edition rather than quoting last edition’s answer. (ii) THE 9 SEPTEMBER MARK IS $95.61 — 61 cents ABOVE the trigger, and the first mark on the scored series above $95 since 24 July. It moves nothing, and the reason is the most expensive lesson in this document. §9.31 was written after an edition led on four intraday readings — a forward below its trigger, a breakeven at its anchor, a lapsed threshold, a yield below its auction stop — and every one was false by that day’s close, because the Singapore-morning cut had missed the entire US session in one direction. (!) THE HONEST FORM OF THAT ARGUMENT CUTS AGAINST THIS DOCUMENT AND IS PRINTED ANYWAY. The 8 September snapshot published here read $93.32 and settled $94.38, and eleven of fourteen reconciled fields settled ABOVE their marks — so on this week’s evidence the morning cut UNDERSTATES a rallying tape, which makes $95.61 a conservative reading of the 9 September close rather than an unreliable one. The channel is nevertheless held, and the reason is the rule and not the arithmetic: a mark is not a close, and this document does not move a market channel on one. (iii) The rule is not moved, and the reason is affirmative rather than procedural. The active contract closed $97.92, a FIFTH consecutive close through $95 and the highest active close since 22 May; on COA the upgrade condition was met on 3 September and has been met every session since. But the $95 upgrade, the $72.48 downgrade and the pre-war anchor are ALL written on the continuation, so moving the upgrade alone to the active contract would leave the other two on a different series and make the channel incoherent in the opposite direction (§9.56b). It would also be moving a rule to the series that fires it, seven days after this document disclosed the problem in the open, which is what §9.26 forbids. What settles this is a print, not an argument: two CO2 closes above $95 fire the upgrade 2→3 and take the score to 28. (iv) The basis narrowed on both contracts for the first time in this run — Brent 3.96 to 3.54, WTI 2.91 to 2.84 — so the two moved the same way, which the last two editions expressly could not say. §9.41 clears; §9.36 still forbids constructing anything across the two Brent series. (v) Three dated events sit in the window and no wire attributes the move to any one of them. OPEC+ held October output UNCHANGED on 6 September and next meets 4 October; pre-meeting REPORTING, not the release, says members must first review spare capacity. CENTCOM says it destroyed five Iranian tankers on the 8th. Houthi forces struck four Saudi sites on the 8th, including the 400,000 b/d Jizan refinery — which was ALREADY offline from earlier attacks, so no incremental barrel loss is asserted — with a halt to some operations and 73 wounded. (!) No quantified OPEC+ or IEA spare-capacity figure dated 4–9 September was published or found, and the 0.07 mb/d effective-spare figure this document has carried since 14 August COULD NOT BE RE-CONFIRMED from a primary source this cycle. It is flagged as unrefreshed rather than repeated as current (§9.13).

bondYield.title: US INFLATION IMPULSE — 5/5, held. The breakeven resolved after two editions dark, and it resolved upward; the forward took a fifth close above its firing level.
bondYield.text: (i) The 5y5y forward closed 2.3119%, a FIFTH close above the 2.30% level whose sustained break fired this channel 4→5 on 31 July, clearing by 1.19 bp. The five clearances run 1.10, 0.96, 1.54, 0.82 and 1.19 bp — wider than the fourth, and NOT the widest of the five, which is worth stating because the temptation is to read the latest as the extreme. The scored downgrade, the 2.142% anchor, sits 16.99 bp below and has not been approached. (ii) BE10 RESOLVED, AFTER TWO CONSECUTIVE EDITIONS UNRESOLVED, AND IT RESOLVED THE WAY THE UNDER-CLAIMING RULE PROTECTED AGAINST. On 7 September it was a carry on a shut market (§9.58c); on 8 September this document reported a mark of 2.3536 as an exact four-decimal repeat and asserted no change. The 8 September close is 2.3751% — up 2.19 bp on the 4 September close and the highest close since 4 June. Had the repeat been published as a reading, this edition would be reporting a flat breakeven on a session it rose more than two basis points. That is the seventeenth-of-August failure run in reverse, and it is the second time §9.35 has paid on this series in three sessions. (!) No reconciliation entry exists for BE10, because a gap is a mark minus a close and the mark was published unresolved (§9.37). Compensation now sits 11.82 bp above its 2.2569 anchor, from 9.63. (iii) So the honest form of the standing claim has CHANGED, and it changed against the comfortable reading. For three editions this document reported ten-year compensation as flat, bounded to 4 September, and warned that the diesel records and the $97 close fell after that date and were untested. They have now been tested by one close, and compensation rose. One close is a session, not a regime (§9.18) — but the direction is the one the pass-through thesis predicts and the one this document has spent three editions saying it could not see. (iv) It is still only one close, and the corroborating detail cuts both ways: the five-year nominal set a war high on the same session while the thirty-year rose 0.31 bp, so the move is concentrated in the belly and the front, which is a policy-path move at least as much as an inflation move. The Federal Reserve governor whose 3 September remarks are the last word before the blackout said his earlier worry about energy bleeding into goods and services ‘hasn’t come to pass, at least so far’ — but he also said it might not take much acceleration to nudge him toward supporting tighter policy, and that his vote turns on the August inflation data. Both halves are quoted because the second is the half consistent with the pricing below. That data lands on 11 September, two days after this edition and inside the blackout. (v) The pricing supports a SIGN and not a number. The readings are hike-or-hold and none prices a cut above 1%: a 52% hike on a prediction market and 57.4% from a futures-implied model, both dated 8 September; 44.5% HOLD on two prediction markets dated the 9th; a 66% hike from a futures tool dated 31 August. A fifth figure, a cross-venue volume-weighted 54.2%, is a DERIVED construct and not a venue reading; it is recorded rather than used. (!) These sit on four incompatible venues with different contracts and methods and are NOT joined, averaged or chained (§9.19); the two 8 September readings, taken on the same day, disagree by about five points. What survives is the sign: the September debate is hike-versus-hold.

bondYield.title: TREASURY STRESS — 5/5, held. The volatility leg has LAPSED for the sixth time in the war, the five-year set a war high, and $119bn of coupons is being absorbed as this is written.
bondYield.text: (i) MOVE RESOLVED at 76.14 on 8 September after going dark on the 7 September row and on the 8 September MARK row — one missed session, two dark rows — and the downgrade’s volatility leg has LAPSED: it fails 75 by 1.14, ending a run of exactly TWO sub-75 closes (3 and 4 September). That is the SIXTH time in this war the leg has been satisfied and given back — single closes on 29 July, 5 August and 7 August, three on 12–14 August, nine on 18–28 August, two now — and it vindicates the refusal to convert two dark rows into a third satisfied close (§9.9). (!) Bound that vindication properly: the downgrade is CONJUNCTIVE and the yield leg has failed since 6 July, so the SCORE was invariant to the MOVE call. What was vindicated is the leg-level statement, not the channel. Volatility is also back ABOVE its own pre-war anchor, by 2.76 points, which retires the ‘fully normalised expectation of movement’ framing for as long as it holds. (ii) The yield leg fails by 24.54 bp, wider than 24.23, and has not closed below 5.00% since 6 July. (!) The bounded form is the only honest one: the pre-war anchor of 4.6106% sits 39 bp INSIDE the condition, so this is a claim about the current regime and not a war-long one. Both legs moved AWAY this session — the first time in three editions that the rotation described by §9.15 has not applied, because nothing rotated. (iii) THE CURVE IS A CLEAN BEAR FLATTENER AND, THIS TIME, IT IS MONOTONIC — which is stated only because the last edition’s draft asserted monotonicity on numbers that contradicted it. From the 4 September close to the 8 September close, one settled session across four calendar days: 2Y +2.75 bp, 5Y +1.79, 10Y +0.61, 20Y +0.52, 30Y +0.31, each smaller than the one before it, with 2s10s −2.14 bp to the flattest close since 28 August. The five-year closed 4.5627%, a NEW WAR HIGH, taking out 4.5551 of 1 September by 0.76 bp; every other tenor’s war high survives, the 2-year’s by 0.62 bp. (!) The 9 September mark repeats the five-year to four decimals and is UNRESOLVED, so the record is not extended and no d/d is asserted (§9.35). A front-led flattening into a September FOMC priced for a hike is a policy-path curve, and it is the shape a war-driven term-premium story does NOT predict. (iv) The supply test is running now and the first leg cleared without incident. The $58bn 3-year of 8 September cleared 4.474% at a bid-to-cover of 2.72, with indirects 62.15%, directs 26.94% and primary dealers 10.91% — on the COMPETITIVE-ACCEPTED denominator of $57.619bn; on total award ex-SOMA those read 61.74, 26.77 and 10.84, and the two bases are never compared with one another (§9.40). A dealer take under 11% is the composition reading that matters and it is a comfortable one (§9.29). (!) NO TAIL IS ASSERTED and none can be: Treasury publishes no when-issued level (§9.39). (v) The $39bn 10-year reopening auctions on 9 September and the $22bn 30-year on the 10th — $119bn of coupons settling 15 September, FOMC day one. Results for neither exist at the cut: PROSPECTIVE. August CPI lands 11 September, inside the blackout.

bondYield.title: POLITICAL STRESS — 5/5, held. The scored series is unresolved for a third session, and the diesel record run it could not see ended by three hundredths of a cent.
bondYield.text: (i) The scored series has NO RESOLVED OBSERVATION SINCE 4 SEPTEMBER. Its 7 September cell repeats $4.93 exactly on a market that was shut, which is §9.58c; 8 and 9 September are blank. (!) §9.48 is applied and stated rather than assumed: AUTMUSAG is a TWO-decimal retail series that repeats values genuinely — $4.82 ran four consecutive sessions in August — so an exact repeat carries far less improbability here than on a four-decimal yield, and the rule is being run where it discriminates weakly. Nothing turns on it: the distance to the $4.60 condition is 33 cents on either reading, and the condition needs THREE closes at or below it with no intervening print above $4.70, so the earliest possible downgrade is at least three prints away. The series is not extrapolated through the dark cells (§9.30). (ii) THE RECORD RUN ENDED, AND IT ENDED BY THREE HUNDREDTHS OF A CENT. AAA’s national diesel average printed $5.9012 for 8 September against the $5.9015 it set on the 7th. After all-time highs on 4, 6 and 7 September this is a first down-day, and the record STANDS at the 7 September level rather than being taken a fourth time. The 9 September national averages had not posted at the cut. (iii) A CORRECTION, AND IT IS THIS DOCUMENT’S OWN §9.57 FAILING IN A NEW PLACE. The last edition set AAA’s gasoline record and the scored series’ own peak in adjacent sentences. They are different series: $5.18 on 20 May is AUTMUSAG’s war high, and AAA’s all-time regular record is $5.0165 of 14 June 2022. Neither is evidence about the other. On its own terms AUTMUSAG at $4.93 is 4.83% below its war high, while AAA regular at $4.1514 is 17.2% below its 2022 record — two very different distances, and printing them side by side without the labels was the error. (iv) Gasoline still does not follow diesel. On AAA’s week-ago base diesel is +26.87c and regular +5.60c, roughly five times the pace and a fourth consecutive edition of it. (!) A FIFTH retail series is not spliced in: EIA on-highway diesel read $5.599 for 31 August against an EIA all-time high of $5.810, so on the EIA survey the record has still NOT been taken (§9.19). Its delayed print was due 9 September and had not published at the cut. (v) THE SCOPE QUESTION STAYS OPEN AND IS NOT DECIDED HERE. AUTMUSAG is a GASOLINE series and the records were in DIESEL; the channel cannot register a distillate record BY CONSTRUCTION, which is a scope choice and not an instrument failure (§9.61). Whether the political channel should be scored on a distillate series is a real question, and §9.21 and §9.56b forbid settling it on an edition that is watching the record it cannot see reverse.

bondYield.title: ESCALATION RISK — 5/5, held. The kinetic record this document called empty was not empty, the war widened to four Saudi sites, and the mediator published three times without mentioning the strait.
bondYield.text: (i) THE CENTRAL FACT OF THIS WINDOW IS A WITHDRAWAL. The last edition reported no CENTCOM release since 5 September and built an ‘empty kinetic record’ on it. CENTCOM released on 8 September: it SAYS it destroyed FIVE Iranian crude carriers, four in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg, after the IRGC targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles twice in two days. (!) That is a battle-damage claim by a party to the conflict and no allied product corroborates it — JMIC 094 predates it — and it is labelled here on the same terms as Iran’s. The item was unreachable from the release index, which served a stale listing topping out at 5 September, and was reachable only with an explicit page parameter. (!) The lesson is §9.23’s, in its most literal form: a negative claim about a source is a claim about the SOURCE, and a cached index is not the source. The claim was load-bearing for a scenario line and it was wrong. (ii) The escalation is one of scale as well as fact. Three Iranian tankers claimed destroyed on 5 September, FIVE on the 8th; Iranian ballistic missiles fired at US warships in both windows; Adm. Brad Cooper framing it explicitly as raising the economic cost, though in a ratio — three of theirs for two of ours — that describes the 5 September action rather than the five-vessel one announced with it. This is navy-on-navy for a second time in four days, and eight Iranian vessels are claimed destroyed across the two exchanges. (iii) What IS still true is narrower and must be stated narrowly: no acknowledged US strike on Iranian SOIL from 1 September through 8 September, an eighth day — and 9 September is unreported at the cut on every track, so it is NOT counted. The strikes were on tankers in waters near Kharg, not on the island; no damage ashore is reported. (!) Iran’s 5 September claim to have struck three tankers stays UNCORROBORATED into a fifth day; no allied product records it, which is not the same as saying it did not happen. (iv) THE WAR WIDENED, AND IT WIDENED TO A GULF STATE. On 8 September Houthi forces struck Abha International Airport, King Khalid Air Base and Aramco facilities at Abha and Jizan — four sites, 73 wounded, the 400,000 b/d Jizan refinery among them and operations temporarily suspended by the energy ministry. (!) The Jizan plant was ALREADY offline from earlier attacks, and the ministry reported a halt to SOME operations — so no incremental barrel loss is asserted and the 400,000 b/d figure is capacity, not lost supply. It is described as the heaviest such attack in years and follows the collapse of a four-year truce; Saudi Arabia struck Taiz and Marib in reply the same day. The US Secretary of State said on the 8th that the Iranian hand is behind it. (!) That attribution is a STATEMENT and is not treated as establishing Iranian direction; the scenario line below turns on the fact of Gulf-state infrastructure being struck, which is not in dispute. (v) THE MEDIATOR IS THE MISSING SIGNATURE FOR A THIRD CONSECUTIVE EDITION, AND THE NEGATIVE IS AT ITS STRONGEST YET. Iran’s security-council secretary said the maps are agreed and will be signed within days; its foreign ministry said the deal is in final stages and the understanding will be lodged with the IMO within days. (!) Both are TIER 3 state media, uncorroborated, and no IMO filing is asserted. (!) Method, stated exactly (§9.23c): fm.gov.om homepage and its English news archive, read direct on 9 September, asked whether ANY item touches Hormuz, Iran, navigation or the arrangement. Answer: none. The ministry published THREE items on 8 September — on Israeli settlements, a Rwandan state visit, and a condemnation of the attacks on Saudi Arabia — so it commented on the region that day and not on this, from a site whose footer reads last updated 8 September. Its foreign minister’s signed newspaper article of 6 September says no solution has been reached and Oman is not walking away: a holding line, and the only Omani ministerial word in the window. An instrument announced by one party, unacknowledged by the second while that second speaks on other subjects, and rejected in advance by the third is not a mediated pause. The channel has been at 5/5 since 9 July and can register none of it (§9.7).

(!) §9.49, the recorded DEFECT, is now WORSE rather than merely unchanged: B has been satisfied across SEVEN closes spanning THREE of the four curve configurations available — bear flattener, bear steepener and bull steepener; only a bull flattener has never occurred under it. A test meant to detect long-end stress has returned the same answer through all three

NOT ARMED, and RESOLVED after two dark sessions: MOVE closed 76.14, 53.86 points below C and 38.88 below the 115.02 war high of 26 March. (!) The Treasury downgrade’s volatility leg has LAPSED on the same print, a SIXTH satisfied-then-given-back sequence (§9.18). (!) The two anchor deviations are reported SEPARATELY and no composite is constructed: volatility is now 2.76 points ABOVE its 73.38 anchor, having been below it, and the 30-year 63.48 bp ABOVE its 4.6106 anchor. The war’s standing anomaly — normalised volatility around an un-normalised yield — has weakened on the volatility side for the first time since 28 August
analysis.crossAsset: ¶ THE MACRO WINDOW IS THIN AND THE FED IS SILENT: 7 September was a federal holiday, the blackout opened on 5 September, and NO Federal Reserve speech occurred 4–9 September — a CONFIRMED ABSENCE. No scheduled US macro data was released in the window. PPI lands 10 SEPTEMBER and CPI 11 SEPTEMBER, both inside the blackout; the FOMC meets 15–16 September with projections. ¶ (!) §9.28’S FOLLOW-UP TEST DOES NOT DISCRIMINATE ON THE LEVEL. August imports of 7.3 mb/d against a 6.3 four-week average were the routing signal; on the 28 August week — which PRECEDES this window — they read 6.8, exactly equidistant between the two hypotheses. What HAS collapsed is the spread to the four-week average, from 1.0 mb/d to 0.1, though the average itself ROSE. Crude DREW 4.5 mn bbl on 98% utilisation; SPR 286.6 mn bbl, −3.1 mn, delivery against the March commitment rather than a new decision. The test is re-set on the 10 September WPSR. ¶ The September STEO, the delayed EIA retail print and the WPSR were all due in this window and none had published at the cut: PROSPECTIVE.
